title: RAG: chunking, embeddings and hybrid search
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: How documents are split into chunks, embedded, indexed and searched: chunk-count arithmetic, cosine similarity, BM25 plus vectors, reciprocal rank fusion and reranking.
source: LangChain text-splitter docs; Cormack et al. RRF paper (SIGIR 2009); Liu et al. Lost in the Middle (2023); Pinecone and Weaviate learning centre; Robertson BM25; Sentence-Transformers docs

questions.prompt: A document has 2000 tokens. You split it with a sliding window of chunk size 500 tokens and overlap 100 tokens (stride 400); the last chunk may be shorter. How many chunks are produced?
questions.explanation: Chunks start at 0, 400, 800, 1200 and 1600. The fifth chunk covers 1600-2000 (the window would reach 2100, so it is cut at the end). A sixth would start at 2000 with nothing left. General rule: ceil((L - overlap) / (size - overlap)) when L > size.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Adding a modest overlap between consecutive chunks reduces the chance that an answer split across a boundary is lost.
questions.reason: The overlapping text is present in both neighbouring chunks, so either chunk can carry the full sentence or idea.

whys.a: Correct: the duplicated region keeps boundary-straddling content intact in at least one chunk.
whys.b: R is not merely a side fact here; it is exactly the mechanism.
whys.c: R is true: overlap duplicates text in both chunks.
whys.d: A is true; overlap is the standard mitigation for boundary cuts.

questions.explanation: Typical overlap is 10-20% of the chunk size. More overlap costs storage, embedding spend and duplicate hits in the results.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Making chunks as large as possible always improves retrieval precision.
questions.reason: Larger chunks give the generator more surrounding context for each retrieved passage.

whys.a: A is false, so no explanation can rescue it.
whys.b: A is false, so the pair cannot be both-true.
whys.c: R is true, so this option is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: big chunks blur many topics into one embedding, which lowers precision, even though they do give more context.

questions.explanation: Chunk size is a trade-off: small chunks give sharp embeddings but lose context; large chunks keep context but dilute the vector. Parent-document retrieval tries to get both.

questions.prompt: Match each chunking strategy to what it does.

right.text: Cuts every N characters or tokens regardless of structure
Tries separators in order (paragraph, line, space, character) until pieces fit the size
Embeds sentences and starts a new chunk where adjacent similarity drops
Indexes small child chunks but returns the larger parent passage to the LLM
Splits at heading boundaries and keeps the section title as metadata
Re-scores the top results with a cross-encoder

questions.explanation: Fixed-size is the cheapest baseline; recursive is the common default; semantic costs extra embedding calls; parent-document and header-based exploit document structure.

questions.prompt: Using LangChain, write Python that creates a RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with chunk_size 800, chunk_overlap 100 and the separators paragraph break, newline, space, then empty string (in that order).

checks.label: lists separators from paragraph down to empty string

questions.model:
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=800,
    chunk_overlap=100,
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", " ", ""],
)
chunks = splitter.split_text(text)
questions.explanation: By default the size is measured in characters (len), not tokens; use from_tiktoken_encoder to count tokens. chunk_overlap must be smaller than chunk_size or the splitter raises a ValueError. The separators list is also the default order.

questions.prompt: Two 2-dimensional embeddings are a = (3, 4) and b = (4, 3). Compute cosine similarity multiplied by 100.
questions.explanation: dot = 3*4 + 4*3 = 24 and both norms are 5, so cosine = 24/25 = 0.96. Cosine ignores vector length and measures only direction.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: For L2-normalised embeddings, ranking by cosine similarity gives the same order as ranking by dot product.
questions.reason: Cosine similarity always lies between -1 and 1.

whys.a: R is true but it is a range property; it says nothing about why the orders match.
whys.b: Correct: with unit vectors the denominators are 1, so cosine equals the dot product. The -1 to 1 range is true but unrelated to that.
whys.c: R is true, so A-true-R-false is wrong.
whys.d: A is true: that is why many vector DBs offer a fast dot-product index on normalised vectors.

questions.explanation: Many embedding APIs return normalised vectors, so a dot-product index is equivalent to cosine and slightly cheaper.

questions.prompt: Why do production vector stores use approximate nearest neighbour indexes such as HNSW instead of exact search?

options.text: Brute force scales linearly with corpus size; ANN trades some recall for speed.
options.why: Right: HNSW and IVF cut the search space and expose recall-vs-speed knobs like ef_search or nprobe.

options.text: ANN indexes return exactly the same top-k as brute force while using much less disk space.
options.why: ANN is approximate; some true neighbours can be missed.

options.text: Exact search cannot be combined with cosine similarity, only with Euclidean distance.
options.why: Brute-force cosine search works; it is just slow at scale.

options.text: HNSW removes the need to embed documents because it indexes the raw text directly.
options.why: Documents are still embedded; the index only organises vectors.

questions.explanation: Interviewers like the follow-up: measure recall of the ANN index against brute force on a sample before trusting it.

questions.prompt: Complete the description of hybrid search.
questions.text: Hybrid search runs {1} (lexical) and vector search separately and merges the two rankings with {2}, which uses only ranks, so the different score scales need no normalisation.
questions.explanation: BM25 is strong on exact tokens such as IDs and error codes; vectors are strong on paraphrase. RRF is the common, tuning-free merge.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A query for the exact error code "ERR-40417" is usually served better by BM25 than by a dense embedding alone.
questions.reason: BM25 scores documents by meaning, so synonyms of the query score highly.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, not merely unrelated.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because rare exact tokens are strong lexical signals, but BM25 is lexical (term frequency and rarity), not semantic.
whys.d: A is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.explanation: Dense models can blur rare identifiers. Hybrid search covers both failure modes.

questions.prompt: With reciprocal rank fusion, score = sum over lists of 1/(k + rank) and k = 60. A document is rank 1 in the BM25 list and rank 2 in the vector list. Give its fused score multiplied by 10000, rounded to the nearest integer.
questions.explanation: 1/61 + 1/62 = 0.016393 + 0.016129 = 0.032522, times 10000 is about 325.2. The constant k damps the advantage of being first.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function rrf(rankings, k=60) where rankings is a list of ranked lists of document ids (best first). Return the document ids sorted by fused RRF score, highest first.
questions.explanation: Other solutions pass (defaultdict, 0-based enumerate with k + rank + 1). Ties are broken arbitrarily unless you add a secondary key.

questions.text: A {1} reads the query and document together in one forward pass, which is more accurate but too slow for the whole corpus, so it reorders only the top-k candidates from the fast {2} first stage.
questions.explanation: Bi-encoders embed query and documents separately, so document vectors are precomputed. Cross-encoders cannot be precomputed per document.

questions.prompt: Your retriever returns the correct chunk, but at rank 18 of the top 20, so the LLM context (top 4) misses it. What is the cheapest targeted fix?

options.text: Rerank the top 20 candidates with a cross-encoder and keep the best 4.
options.why: Right: the recall is fine, the ordering is the problem, and a reranker fixes ordering.

options.text: Re-embed the whole corpus with a model that has more dimensions, accepting a full reindex.
options.why: Recall is already fine; this is expensive and may not change ordering.

options.text: Raise the LLM temperature so it explores other chunks in the prompt more freely.
options.why: Temperature does not change which chunks are retrieved.

options.text: Increase the chunk size to 4000 tokens so that fewer chunks compete for the top positions.
options.why: Bigger chunks dilute embeddings and can make precision worse.

questions.explanation: Diagnose first: recall@20 high but recall@4 low means a ranking problem, so rerank. Low recall@20 would mean fixing chunking or adding hybrid search.

questions.prompt: Which statements about operating an embedding index are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Queries and documents must be embedded with the same model (or a model trained for the pair).
options.why: Right: vectors from different models live in different spaces.

options.text: Changing the embedding model means re-embedding the whole corpus.
options.why: Right: old vectors are not comparable with new ones.

options.text: Vectors from two different models can be stored in one index and compared.
options.why: Their dimensions and geometry differ; similarities are meaningless.

options.text: Cosine similarity of 0.8 means 80% of the words match.
options.why: Similarity is geometric, not a word-overlap percentage.

questions.explanation: Version the embedding model name in index metadata so a migration is a planned reindex, not a surprise.

questions.prompt: You store 1,000,000 embeddings of 1536 dimensions as 32-bit floats (4 bytes each), with no compression and no index overhead. How many decimal gigabytes do the raw vectors need, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 1,000,000 x 1536 x 4 bytes = 6.144 GB. An HNSW graph adds extra memory per vector, so budget more; scalar or product quantisation and lower-dimensional models cut the footprint.

questions.prompt: You pass 10 retrieved chunks to the LLM in one prompt. Given the findings on how models use long contexts, where should the strongest chunks go?

options.text: At the start and end of the context block, weaker ones in the middle.
options.why: Right: Liu et al. found accuracy is highest when relevant text sits at the beginning or end and dips in the middle.

options.text: In the middle, so the model reads them with the most surrounding text.
options.why: The middle is where models use information least reliably, so this is the worst position.

options.text: Sorted alphabetically by document title for a stable prompt.
options.why: Alphabetical order ignores relevance, so strong chunks may land in the weak middle region.

options.text: Anywhere, because position never affects long-context accuracy.
options.why: Position does matter: the 'lost in the middle' study measured a U-shaped accuracy curve.

questions.explanation: Reorder after reranking (best first and last) and keep k small; fewer, better chunks beat padding the prompt.
